newsitem.title: USA: Dollar rises in tandem with bonds and stocks.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rises in tandem with bonds and stocks.

text.p: The dollar rose along with surging U.S. bond and stock prices Friday, aided by surprisingly low U.S. inflation and retail sales data which dampened market forecasts of a Federal Reserve interest rate increase.
But after the data, the dollar struggled to exceed fresh eight-week highs set earlier against the German mark and Japanese yen.
Traders expressed concern that the fall in U.S. interest rates, which move in the opposite direction from bond prices, might undermine demand for dollars.
"The underpinning is provided by the bond and stock market," said Ben Strauss, assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer & Co.
"It's keeping the dollar from collapsing because clearly those numbers were bearish as far as interest rates are concered."
U.S. Treasury bonds soared almost 1-1/2 half points after the government said consumer prices rose a slight 0.1 percent and retail sales advanced a tepid 0.2 percent in August.
On Friday, the dollar was at 1.5134 marks, up from 1.5130 marks late Thursday, and at 110.47 yen, up from 110.13 yen.
Wall street economists had expected retail prices to rise 0.2 percent and sales to rise 0.7 percent.

The dollar has posted new highs each day for a week amid speculation that the Federal Reserve would raise short-term interest rates slightly to keep too rapid a pace of economic expansion from generating faster inflation.
Prospects for higher U.S. interest rates often bolsters demand for dollars by making dollar-based deposit rates more attractive.
"The Fed may not move," said Strauss. "That is going to be good for bonds and stocks but clearly puts a damper here on the dollar."

The Dow Jones Industrial stock average rose almost 67 points to a new record high on Friday, in response to hopes the Fed may not act to slow the economy when its policy-making body meets on September 24.
Technical buying of dollars against the Swiss franc and yen led the way higher, traders said.
The dollar closed 1.2435 Swiss, up from 1.2375 on Thursday.
The dollar rose to 110.52 against the yen, its highest since July 15, after Japan's economy fell 0.7 percent in the April through June quarter.
Japan's struggles to emerge from a prolonged recession have all but eliminated chances of interest rates in Japan rising from near-record lows this year.
"Japan's economy is still muddling along," said David Gilmore, partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics. "So that is going to be bearish for yen for the next month or so."
In other trade, the dollar was at Canadian $1.3699, down from C$1.3719.
The pound closed at $1.5553, off from $1.5555 late Thursday.
